title: Refined Noether normalization at a prime
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $n\ge0$, and let $\mathfrak q\subset k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a prime ideal. Put $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, with residue field and transcendence degree as in [def-weil-residue-field, def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Then there exists a finite $k$-algebra homomorphism $\varphi:k[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\to k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] such that $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=(y_{r+1},\ldots,y_n)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 051P (lemma-refined-Noether-normalization), statement and induction proof

proof.text: Use induction on $n$, strengthening the claim by $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak q)\le n$ and finiteness of this transcendence degree. From [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], for any prime $\mathfrak a\subset R$ the map $R_{\mathfrak a}/\mathfrak aR_{\mathfrak a}\to\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak a)$ sends the class of $u/v$ to $\bar u/\bar v$; its inverse sends $\bar u/\bar v$ to that class, since $\bar v\ne0$ means $v\notin\mathfrak a$. Thus we may use this fraction-field description of residue fields. If $\mathfrak q=0$, the variables in $\operatorname{Frac}(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n])$ are algebraically independent (a nonzero polynomial remains nonzero) and generate this field as a field. They are therefore a transcendence basis, so [def-kun-transcendence-degree] gives $r=n$. The polynomial ring is a domain: the product of lexicographically leading nonzero monomials has nonzero coefficient, since $k$ is a field. The variable-renaming isomorphism has zero contraction and is finite, generated as a module by $1$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. This also settles $n=0$, since a field has no prime ideal other than zero. The polynomial operations and variable renaming here are those of [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring].

source.place: Tag 051P, induction and zero-prime case, lines 28082-28085; explicit residue-field fraction description

proof.text: Now $n>0$ and $\mathfrak q\ne0$. Choose $0\ne g\in\mathfrak q$; it is nonconstant because a nonzero scalar is a unit and $\mathfrak q$ is proper. Apply [lem-trf-polynomial-shear-leading-coefficient] with $R=k$. Let $\sigma$ send $x_i$ to $x_i+x_n^{e_i}$ for $i<n$ and fix $x_n$. This is a $k$-algebra automorphism: substitution $x_i\mapsto x_i-x_n^{e_i}$ fixes $x_n$ and is its inverse, as checking each generator shows [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Write $\mathfrak q^*=\sigma(\mathfrak q)$. Its residue field is $k$-isomorphic to that of $\mathfrak q$ by $\bar u/\bar v\mapsto\overline{\sigma(u)}/\overline{\sigma(v)}$. If $a\in k^\times$ is the scalar leading coefficient from the lemma, then $f=a^{-1}\sigma(g)\in\mathfrak q^*$ is monic of positive degree $d$ in $x_n$. We will construct a map with contraction prescribed for $\mathfrak q^*$ and then compose with $\sigma^{-1}$.

source.place: Tag 051P, choice of a nonzero polynomial and triangular automorphism, lines 28085-28095; Tag 051N (lemma-helper-polynomial)

proof.text: Put $B=k[y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}]$, $C=B[y_n]$, and $A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Define $\psi:C\to A$ by $y_i\mapsto x_i$ for $i<n$ and $y_n\mapsto f$, using [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Write $f=x_n^d+\sum_{j<d}c_j(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})x_n^j$. The $C$-algebra $A$ is generated by $x_n$ alone, and this generator is a root of the monic polynomial $$T^d+\sum_{j<d}c_j(y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1})T^j-y_n\in C[T].$$ Therefore [lem-weil-pbc-finite-of-integral-generators] makes $\psi$ finite. Concretely, repeated replacement of $x_n^d$ by $f-\sum_{j<d}c_j(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})x_n^j$ shows that $1,x_n,\ldots,x_n^{d-1}$ generate $A$ over $C$.

source.place: Tag 051P, the finite map with last coordinate f, lines 28095-28103; Tag 02JJ (lemma-characterize-finite-in-terms-of-integral)

proof.text: Let $Q=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q^*)\subset C$ and $\mathfrak p=Q\cap B$. Both are prime: inverse image preserves properness and the condition that a product in the ideal has a factor in it. Since $f\in\mathfrak q^*$, we have $y_n\in Q$. For $H\in C$ write $H=H(y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1},0)+y_nH_1$. Then $\psi(H)$ modulo $\mathfrak q^*$ is the image of the constant coefficient $H(y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1},0)$. Consequently $H\in Q$ if and only if that coefficient belongs to $\mathfrak p$, and $$Q=\mathfrak p C+(y_n).$$ This uses only the polynomial expansion of [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]; it proves the entire contraction assertion, including the reverse inclusion.

source.place: Tag 051P, the equality of the contracted prime with pC+(y_n), lines 28103-28106

proof.text: Write $F=\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak p)$ and $E=\kappa(\mathfrak q^*)=\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak q^*)$ using the fraction maps in Step 1 [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. The map $B/\mathfrak p\to A/\mathfrak q^*$ is injective by the definition of $\mathfrak p$, so [lem-weil-pbc-fraction-field-lift] embeds $F$ into $E$. If $\xi$ denotes the class of $x_n$, then $f\in\mathfrak q^*$ gives a monic degree-$d$ equation for $\xi$ over $F$. Thus $D=F[\xi]\subset E$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-of-integral-generators]. It is a domain as a subring of the field $E$, so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dimensional-domain-is-field] makes it a field. Every class in $A/\mathfrak q^*$ is a polynomial in $\xi$ over $B/\mathfrak p$, hence lies in $D$. Since $D$ is a field, all fractions of these classes lie in $D$, giving $E=D$. In particular $E/F$ is finite.

source.place: Tag 051P, finiteness of the residue extension, lines 28106-28108; explicit monogenic field argument

proof.text: Every $z\in E$ is algebraic over $F$: if $N=\dim_F E$, the $N+1$ vectors $1,z,\ldots,z^N$ are linearly dependent, and a nonzero list of dependence coefficients gives a nonzero polynomial vanishing at $z$. The tower formula and algebraicity clause of [lem-kun-transcendence-degree-tower] now give $$\operatorname{trdeg}_k E=\operatorname{trdeg}_k F+0.$$ The $k$-isomorphism in Step 2 identifies $\operatorname{trdeg}_k E$ with the original $r$: polynomial relations correspond in both directions under that isomorphism. Therefore $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak p)=r$.

source.place: Tag 051P, equality of residue transcendence degrees, lines 28107-28108; Fields Tag 030H (lemma-transcendence-degree-tower)

proof.text: Apply the induction hypothesis to the prime $\mathfrak p$ of the $(n-1)$-variable ring $B$. This shows $r\le n-1$ and supplies a finite $k$-algebra map $$\beta:k[z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1}]\to B,\qquad \beta^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=(z_{r+1},\ldots,z_{n-1}).$$ Extend it to $\widetilde\beta:k[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\to C$ by $z_n\mapsto y_n$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. This extension is finite without any additional base-change assertion: if $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ generate $B$ as a module over $k[z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1}]$ via $\beta$, expand every coefficient of $\sum_j h_jy_n^j$ as $h_j=\sum_i\beta(a_{ij})b_i$. Then the polynomial equals $\sum_i\widetilde\beta(\sum_j a_{ij}z_n^j)b_i$. The same finite list $b_i$ therefore generates $C$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module].

source.place: Tag 051P, apply the induction hypothesis and extend by the last variable, lines 28109-28117

proof.text: For $H\in k[z_1,\ldots,z_n]$, reduction modulo $y_n$ sends $\widetilde\beta(H)$ to $\beta(H(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1},0))$. By Step 4, $\widetilde\beta(H)\in Q$ if and only if this last element is in $\mathfrak p$; by Step 7 this means $H(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1},0)\in(z_{r+1},\ldots,z_{n-1})$. Subtracting this constant term leaves a multiple of $z_n$, so this is equivalent to $$H\in(z_{r+1},\ldots,z_{n-1})k[z_1,\ldots,z_n]+(z_n)=(z_{r+1},\ldots,z_n).$$ Thus $\widetilde\beta^{-1}(Q)$ is exactly the required coordinate ideal. The reduction and divisibility by the last variable are coefficient identities in [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring].

source.place: Tag 051P, verification of the final composite contraction, lines 28117-28122

proof.text: Define $\varphi=\sigma^{-1}\circ\psi\circ\widetilde\beta$. The maps $\widetilde\beta$ and $\psi$ are finite by Steps 7 and 3. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-module-over-finite-algebra] with the last ring as its own module to see that their composite is finite. The automorphism $\sigma^{-1}$ is finite as well: every element $a\in A$ is $\sigma^{-1}(\sigma(a))\cdot1$, so its target module is generated by $1$. A second application of the same cited statement makes $\varphi$ finite. Since $(\sigma^{-1})^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\sigma(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak q^*$, Steps 4 and 8 give $$\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\widetilde\beta^{-1}(\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q^*))=(z_{r+1},\ldots,z_n).$$ Rename $z_i$ as $y_i$ to obtain the stated map. All maps fix $k$, and the bound $r\le n-1\le n$ proves the strengthening used for induction.

lean.statement: theorem refinedNoetherNormalizationPrime (k : Type u) [Field k] (n : ℕ) (q : Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin n) k)) [q.IsPrime] : ∃ r : ℕ, Algebra.trdeg k q.ResidueField = (r : Cardinal) ∧ r ≤ n ∧ ∃ φ : MvPolynomial (Fin n) k →ₐ[k] MvPolynomial (Fin n) k, φ.toRingHom.Finite ∧ Ideal.comap φ.toRingHom q = Ideal.span (Set.range (fun i : Fin n => if r ≤ i.1 then MvPolynomial.X i else 0))
